traditions/korean-methodist-church/summa: Methodism reached Korea with American missionaries Henry Appenzeller and William Scranton in 1885. In 1930 the northern and southern American Methodist missions united to form the autonomous Korean Methodist Church. Korean Methodists were prominent in the 1919 independence movement, and the church grew dramatically after the Korean War.
traditions/korean-methodist-church/profi: Scripture with Methodist doctrinal standards and Korean confessional statements.
Episcopal with bishops elected for set terms.
Methodist liturgy with Korean revival prayer practices.
traditions/korean-methodist-church/statu: Active; one of the largest Methodist churches in Asia.
traditions/church-of-god-in-christ/summa: Founded in 1897 in Mississippi by Charles Harrison Mason and Charles Price Jones as a holiness church. After Mason received Spirit baptism at the Azusa Street revival in 1907, the church divided; Mason's Pentecostal majority kept the name, and Jones's group became the Church of Christ (Holiness). For years COGIC was one of the few incorporated Pentecostal bodies able to ordain clergy, including many white ministers. Headquartered in Memphis, it is the largest Pentecostal denomination in the United States and a pillar of African American church life; Martin Luther King Jr. gave his final 'Mountaintop' speech at its Mason Temple in 1968.
traditions/church-of-god-in-christ/disti: Black-led church founded by former slaves' children
Women's Department as a powerful parallel structure
traditions/church-of-god-in-christ/profi: Scripture as inspired Word; COGIC Official Manual.

Salvation by grace through faith, sanctification and baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience subsequent to conversion, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues; gifts of healing and prophecy for today.
Baptism by immersion, the Lord's Supper and feet washing as ordinances.
Episcopal: Presiding Bishop, General Board, jurisdictional bishops; women serve as evangelists and missionaries but not as pastors or bishops.
Ecstatic worship with shouting, tarrying, testimony and gospel choirs.
traditions/church-of-god-in-christ/statu: Active; one of the largest Pentecostal bodies in North America.
traditions/church-of-god-cleveland/summa: Traces its origins to the Christian Union formed by Richard Spurling at Barney Creek, Tennessee, in 1886, and the 1896 Shearer Schoolhouse revival in North Carolina. Under A. J. Tomlinson it became Pentecostal after G. B. Cashwell, back from Azusa Street, preached in Cleveland in 1908. A 1923 dispute led to Tomlinson's Church of God of Prophecy. Now a large worldwide church.
traditions/church-of-god-cleveland/disti: Oldest Pentecostal denomination in the U.S. by founding date
traditions/church-of-god-cleveland/profi: Scripture as the Word of God, "rightly divided"; Declaration of Faith (1948).
Justification, sanctification and baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience subsequent to conversion, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues; gifts of healing and prophecy for today.
Baptism by immersion, the Lord's Supper and feet washing.
Centralised: General Assembly and General Overseer appoint state overseers.
traditions/church-of-god-cleveland/statu: Active; worldwide membership in the millions.
traditions/foursquare-church/name: International Church of the Foursquare Gospel
traditions/foursquare-church/summary: Founded by the evangelist Aimee Semple McPherson, who opened Angelus Temple in Los Angeles in 1923 and incorporated the denomination in 1927. A pioneer of religious radio and of social relief during the Depression, she preached the 'Foursquare Gospel' of Jesus as Saviour, Baptiser with the Holy Spirit, Healer and Coming King.
traditions/foursquare-church/distinctive: Founded and led by a woman
Foursquare Gospel (adapted from A. B. Simpson)
Early use of radio and dramatic sermons
Strong in Brazil, the Philippines and Nigeria
traditions/foursquare-church/profile/aut: Scripture; the Declaration of Faith written by McPherson.
traditions/foursquare-church/profile/sal: Salvation by grace through faith; Baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience subsequent to conversion, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues; gifts of healing and prophecy for today.
traditions/foursquare-church/profile/sac: Baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
traditions/foursquare-church/profile/gov: Central board and president with district supervisors.
traditions/apostolic-church/summary: A Pentecostal church formed in 1916 at Penygroes, Carmarthenshire, by Daniel Powell Williams, a convert of the 1904–05 Welsh Revival. It recognises the present-day offices of apostle and prophet (Ephesians 4:11) and gives a central place to directive prophecy in church government. Its missions made it large in Nigeria and Ghana.
traditions/apostolic-church/distinctives: Restored offices of apostle and prophet
traditions/apostolic-church/profile/auth: Scripture as final authority, with prophetic guidance in church affairs tested by it.
traditions/apostolic-church/profile/salv: Salvation by grace; Baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience subsequent to conversion, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues; gifts of healing and prophecy for today.
traditions/apostolic-church/profile/sacr: Baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
traditions/apostolic-church/profile/gove: Government by apostles and prophets with elders and deacons.
traditions/apostolic-church/status: Active; largest branches in Nigeria and Ghana.
traditions/elim-pentecostal/summary: Founded in Monaghan, Ireland, in 1915 by the Welsh evangelist George Jeffreys, whose healing campaigns filled the Royal Albert Hall in the 1920s–30s. Elim became one of the main British Pentecostal denominations; Jeffreys left in 1940 over church government. In 1978 missionaries and their families were murdered at an Elim mission in Rhodesia (Vumba).
traditions/elim-pentecostal/distinctives: More centralised than British Assemblies of God
Does not require tongues as the only initial evidence
traditions/elim-pentecostal/profile/auth: Scripture as infallible; Elim Fundamental Truths.
traditions/elim-pentecostal/profile/salv: Salvation by grace; Spirit baptism with signs following.
traditions/elim-pentecostal/profile/sacr: Believers' baptism and the Lord's Supper.
traditions/elim-pentecostal/profile/gove: Connexional, with a General Conference and central leadership.
traditions/pentecostal-assemblies-of-the: Organised in Los Angeles about 1907 and reorganised in 1918 as an interracial Oneness body after merging with the General Assembly of Apostolic Assemblies; Garfield T. Haywood, an African American pastor in Indianapolis, became its first Presiding Bishop in 1925. Most white ministers withdrew in 1924, forming bodies that later became the United Pentecostal Church. It stands outside historic Nicene Trinitarian orthodoxy.
Oneness theology: one God revealed as Father, Son and Spirit, whose name is Jesus
Baptism in the name of Jesus
Scripture; rejects the Nicene doctrine of three persons as unbiblical.
Repentance, baptism in Jesus' name and Spirit baptism with tongues (Acts 2:38) as the new birth.
Baptism by immersion in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord's Supper and feet washing.
Episcopal: Presiding Bishop and diocesan bishops.
traditions/united-pentecostal-church-int: The largest Oneness Pentecostal denomination, formed in St Louis in 1945 by the merger of the Pentecostal Church, Inc. and the Pentecostal Assemblies of Jesus Christ. It teaches that the one God is fully revealed in Jesus Christ and that baptism in Jesus' name and the gift of tongues are part of the new birth. It stands outside historic Nicene Trinitarianism.
Acts 2:38 as the plan of salvation
Strict holiness standards of dress and appearance
Large missions in Latin America and the Philippines
Scripture as the inspired Word; rejects Trinitarian creeds.
Repentance, water baptism in Jesus' name and Spirit baptism with tongues.
Baptism by immersion in Jesus' name, the Lord's Supper and feet washing.
Premillennial rapture and return of Christ.
Congregational churches with a General Conference and General Superintendent.
traditions/assembleias-de-deus-brazil/su: Founded in Belém in 1911 by the Swedish missionaries Daniel Berg and Gunnar Vingren, after their Pentecostal teaching led to expulsion from a Baptist church. Linked historically with Swedish rather than U.S. Pentecostalism, the Assemblies of God in Brazil grew into the country's largest Protestant family, now divided among several large conventions and ministries.
traditions/assembleias-de-deus-brazil/di: Strict traditional usos e costumes in many congregations
Growing political influence in Brazil's evangelical caucus
traditions/assembleias-de-deus-brazil/pr: Scripture; Declaration of Faith of the CGADB.
Salvation by grace through faith; Baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience subsequent to conversion, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues; gifts of healing and prophecy for today.
Baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
Mother churches (ministérios) with pastor-presidents and networks of dependent congregations; national conventions.
traditions/assembleias-de-deus-brazil/st: Active; the largest Pentecostal family in Brazil.
traditions/yoido-full-gospel-church/summ: Begun as a tent church in a Seoul slum in 1958 by David Yonggi Cho and Choi Ja-shil, affiliated with the Assemblies of God. Moving to Yeouido island in 1973, it became the largest single congregation in the world, organised around home cell groups. Cho's 'threefold blessing' (spiritual, physical and material well-being, from 3 John 2) has been criticised as a prosperity gospel; Cho was also convicted of embezzlement in 2014.
traditions/yoido-full-gospel-church/prof: Salvation by grace; Spirit baptism; healing and blessing as fruits of the gospel.
Baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
Senior pastor with elders and cell leaders; affiliated with the Korean Assemblies of God.
Pentecostal worship, all-night and early-morning prayer.
traditions/yoido-full-gospel-church/stat: Active; membership reported in the hundreds of thousands.
traditions/redeemed-christian-church-of-: Founded in Lagos in 1952 by Josiah Akindayomi, who had belonged to the Cherubim and Seraphim. Under Enoch Adejare Adeboye (General Overseer from 1981) it became a Pentecostal megachurch movement planting 'parishes' worldwide, known for the Holy Ghost Congress at Redemption Camp on the Lagos–Ibadan expressway.
Strong diaspora presence in Britain and North America
Scripture; the General Overseer's teaching highly influential.
Salvation by grace, holiness and Spirit baptism.
Baptism by immersion, the Lord's Supper and feet washing in some parishes.
Premillennial rapture and return of Christ.
Hierarchical: General Overseer, regional and provincial pastors.
